units.title: Unit 1: Naming, asking and gender

lessons.title: 1. Э́то, and the verb that isn't there
lessons.subtitle: Saying what things and people are

explanations.title: Э́то
explanations.body: Э́то means “this is”, “that is” or “these are”. It never changes: the same word works for a house, a book or a whole group of people. Put a noun after it and the sentence is finished. In speech, pause briefly after э́то.

examples.translation: This is a house.
This is mom.
This is a window.
These are books.

explanations.title: The verb that isn't there
explanations.body:
English needs “am”, “is” or “are” to join a subject to a description. Russian leaves the present tense of быть (to be) out entirely. You don't say “I am a doctor”; you say, word for word, “I doctor”. That is not shorthand: it is the correct sentence. Only the past and future use быть, and the past comes later in this course.

In writing, two nouns in a row often get a dash (Москва́ — столи́ца, “Moscow is the capital”), but after я, ты, он, она́ and the other pronouns there is none.

examples.translation: I am a doctor.
He is a student.
She is a mom.
We are here.
They are there.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “This is a house”?
exercises.explanation: Э́то + noun is the whole sentence. There is no linking verb to add.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I am a student”?
exercises.explanation: The present tense of быть is simply absent: я студе́нт is complete.
To say “this is…” you use э́то, whatever the noun. Э́та кни́га would only be the phrase “this book”.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a book.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “We are here”?
exercises.explanation: No word for “are”: subject and place are enough.

exercises.prompt: Which word fits every one of these: “This is a window”, “This is a table”, “These are books”?
exercises.explanation: Э́то never changes for gender or number. The others are forms that must agree with a noun.

exercises.prompt: In everyday speech, what goes in the blank?  Он ___ студе́нт.
exercises.explanation: Он студе́нт is already complete. (Явля́ется does mean “is”, but it belongs to formal or scientific writing, like “Вода́ явля́ется жи́дкостью”, not to saying what someone is.)

exercises.prompt: Which of these is NOT correct Russian?
exercises.explanation: Есть is not used to link a subject and a noun in ordinary present-tense sentences.

lessons.title: 2. Asking and answering
lessons.subtitle: Кто? Что? Где? and yes/no questions

explanations.title: Кто? Что? Где?
explanations.body: Кто (who) asks about people. Что (what) asks about things. Где (where) asks about place. These are information questions: they start with a question word, and the voice falls at the end, just as in a statement. Tap a row to hear it.

rows: Who is this? — This is mom.
What is this? — This is a book.
Where is the house? — The house is there.

explanations.title: Yes/no questions
explanations.body: A yes/no question has no question word. It uses the same words as the statement, and only the voice changes: it rises sharply on the word being asked about. In writing, the question mark is the only sign. Tap the speaker on each pair and listen for the rise.

examples.translation: This is a house. (statement)
Is this a house? (question)
Is he a student?
Is mom here?

explanations.title: Short answers
explanations.body: In real conversation people give only the new information. Да and нет can stand alone, or you add the one word that matters. Don't answer an information question with да or нет: it isn't a yes/no question.

exercises.explanation: The answer is a person, so the question is кто.
The answer is a thing, so the question is что.
The answer gives a place, so the question is где.

exercises.prompt: Which question can be answered with да or нет?
exercises.explanation: Only the question without a question word is a yes/no question.

exercises.prompt: How does a yes/no question differ from the matching statement in speech?
options: The voice rises on the word asked about
exercises.explanation: Russian adds nothing. Intonation does the work, which is why listening matters.

exercises.prompt: — Ма́ма здесь?  Pick the natural short answer.
exercises.explanation: Short answers repeat only the new information. “Да, я здесь” would mean “I am here”.

exercises.prompt: — Кто э́то?  Pick the natural short answer.
exercises.explanation: An information question is answered with the information, not with да or нет.
Э́то + noun states what something is.

lessons.title: 3. И or А? And word order
lessons.subtitle: Joining, contrasting, and putting new information last

explanations.title: И and А
explanations.body: Both can be translated as “and”, but Russian chooses by meaning. И joins things that go together or adds one to another. А sets two things against each other, or picks the conversation back up (“and you?”). In the pattern “not X, but Y” you need а.

rows: He is at home, and she is there.
This is not a table but a chair.

explanations.title: Commas, and where the news goes
explanations.body:
Always put a comma before а. Put one before и only when it joins two full clauses (Он здесь, и она́ здесь), not when it joins two words (ма́ма и па́па).

Russian word order is flexible, and the position carries meaning: new or emphasised information usually comes last. So the same two words can answer different questions.

tables.note: The words are the same; the order shows what the speaker is telling you.

exercises.explanation: Mom and dad belong together: и joins them.
In “not X but Y”, Russian uses а.
А picks the conversation back up: “And you?”
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm here. And you?

exercises.explanation: Anna and Boris are being added together, so и.
A comma always comes before а.
No comma when и joins two words.

exercises.prompt: — Что здесь?   Which answer puts the new information last?
exercises.explanation: The question asks what is here, so the thing, кни́га, is the news and comes last.

exercises.prompt: — Где кни́га?   Which answer puts the new information last?
exercises.explanation: The question asks where, so the place, здесь, is the news and comes last.

lessons.title: 4. Gender of nouns
lessons.subtitle: Masculine, feminine, neuter: read it from the ending

explanations.title: Three genders
explanations.body: Every Russian noun is masculine, feminine or neuter, even a table or a window. You can usually tell from the last letter of the dictionary form. Gender matters because other words (my, new, was) change to match the noun, as the next lessons show.

tables.note: Tap a row to hear the words.

explanations.title: Exceptions to learn
explanations.body: Not every noun follows the ending rule. Nouns in a soft sign (-ь) can be masculine or feminine, so learn each one with its gender; two suffixes help: -тель is almost always masculine and -ость always feminine. And a few nouns that name men end in -а or -я but are masculine.

exercises.explanation: It ends in -а, the typical feminine ending.
It looks feminine because of -я, but -мя nouns are neuter: и́мя, вре́мя.
It ends in -а but names a man, so it is masculine: мой па́па.
-ия is a feminine ending. (Compare -ие, as in зда́ние, which is neuter.)

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns is feminine?
exercises.explanation: Ночь is feminine. Soft-sign nouns need to be learned one by one; день and учи́тель are masculine.

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns is masculine?
exercises.explanation: Of the soft-sign nouns here, only день is masculine.

lessons.title: 5. He, she, it: pronouns follow gender
lessons.subtitle: Why a table is он and a book is она́

explanations.title: The eight personal pronouns
explanations.body: Russian has eight personal pronouns. Ты is for one person you are on familiar terms with: a friend, a relative, a child. Вы is for several people, and also for one person you address politely, such as a stranger, a teacher or someone older. Choosing between them is a real social decision.

explanations.title: Он, она́, оно́ replace nouns
explanations.body: A pronoun matches the gender of the noun it replaces, for things as well as people. A table is он, a book is она́, a window is оно́. English calls all three “it”. Plural nouns, of any gender, are replaced by они́. In answers the pronoun is often dropped altogether.

examples.translation: Where is the table? — It is here.
Where is the book? — It is there.
Where is the window? — It is here.
Is your house here? — Yes, it is.

exercises.explanation: Any plural noun is replaced by они́.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are the children? — They are at home.

exercises.explanation: Письмо́ ends in -о, so it is neuter.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to your teacher. Which pronoun do you use for “you”?
exercises.explanation: Вы is the polite form for one person you don't know well, or who deserves respect.

exercises.prompt: You are speaking to two friends together. Which do you use?
exercises.explanation: Ты is only for one person. Several people are always вы.

lessons.title: 6. Possessives and gender
lessons.subtitle: Мой, моя́, моё: match the thing owned, not the owner

explanations.title: My, your, our
explanations.body: The possessives мой, твой, наш and ваш change form to agree in gender with the thing owned. It is the noun that decides, never the owner: a woman says мой брат (masculine) and моя́ сестра́ (feminine) exactly as a man does. Tap a row to hear all three forms.

examples.translation: This is my house.
This is my book.
This is my window.
This is your sister.

explanations.title: Three things to watch
explanations.body:
1. Masculine nouns that end in -а or -я take masculine forms: мой па́па, мой дя́дя.

2. The neuter ends in -ё or -е: моё окно́, на́ше и́мя.

3. Его́ (his), её (her) and их (their) never change, whatever they describe: его́ дом, его́ кни́га, её окно́, их де́ти.

examples.translation: My dad is at home.
This is his book.
This is her brother.

exercises.promptTranslation: This is my sister.
This is my window.

exercises.explanation: Па́па names a man, so it is masculine despite its ending: мой па́па.
exercises.promptTranslation: My dad is at home.
Where is your (polite) book?
This is our house.

exercises.explanation: Её means “her”. It is the only form here that expresses the owner.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is her brother.

exercises.prompt: Which possessive never changes its form?
exercises.explanation: Его́, её and их stay the same for every noun.

exercises.prompt: A woman introduces her brother. Which sentence is right?
exercises.explanation: The owner's gender never matters: брат is masculine, so мой.

exercises.prompt: Which of these nouns takes мой, even though it ends in -а?
exercises.explanation: Па́па is a man, so masculine.

lessons.title: 7. Не or нет?
lessons.subtitle: Negating a word, and saying no

explanations.title: Не negates a word
explanations.body: Не is the negative particle. Put it directly before the word it negates. English needs helpers such as “do not”; Russian just adds не. For now it goes before nouns, adjectives and place words; verbs come later in the course.

examples.translation: This is not my house.
He is not a student.
She is not here.

explanations.title: Нет means “no”
explanations.body: Нет is the word for “no”. It answers a yes/no question, as the opposite of да, and a comma follows it. Notice that Russian uses both: нет answers the question, and не negates the statement.

rows: — Он врач? — Нет, он не врач.

exercises.explanation: Не negates the word after it: “not my house”.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is not my house.

exercises.explanation: To answer “no” you say нет, followed by a comma.
exercises.promptTranslation: — Are you a student? — No, I'm not a student.

exercises.explanation: Не goes before the word it negates.
exercises.promptTranslation: He is not at home.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “She is not a doctor”?
— Ма́ма здесь?  How do you say “No, she isn't”?
exercises.explanation: Нет answers the question (with a comma after it), and не negates здесь.

exercises.prompt: Which word do you use on its own to answer “no”?
exercises.explanation: Не can't stand alone; it always negates a word that follows.
“Not X but Y” is не … а …, with a comma before а.

exercises.prompt: In “Нет, он не врач”, which word negates врач?
exercises.explanation: Нет answers the question; не negates the word врач.

units.title: Unit 2: More than one

lessons.title: 8. Regular plurals
lessons.subtitle: -ы, -и, -а, -я: the ending depends on the last letter

explanations.title: Making a plural
explanations.body: For most nouns the plural ending depends on the last letter of the dictionary form. Tap a row to hear the words. The ending being added is highlighted.

rows: тетра́дь → тетра́д{и}  ·  музе́й → музе́{и}  ·  неде́ля → неде́л{и}

explanations.title: A spelling rule, and a moving stress
explanations.body:
After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ Russian never writes ы: it writes и instead. So кни́га becomes кни́ги (never кни́гы), and нож becomes ножи́.

Also watch the stress. It often moves when the word becomes plural: стол → столы́ (onto the ending), but окно́ → о́кна (back onto the stem). Stress is not written in ordinary Russian text, so learn it together with the word.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of стол?
exercises.explanation: A consonant ending takes -ы: стол → столы́.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of кни́га?
exercises.explanation: Feminine -а normally gives -ы, but after г the spelling rule requires и: кни́ги.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of окно́?
exercises.explanation: Neuter -о becomes -а, and the stress moves back: о́кна.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of неде́ля?
What is the plural of музе́й?
What is the plural of ру́чка?
exercises.explanation: After к, ы is never written: ру́чки.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of зда́ние?
What is the plural of и́мя?
exercises.explanation: Neuter nouns in -мя take -мена, with the stress on the end: имена́. Вре́мя → времена́ works the same way.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of врач?
exercises.explanation: After ч only и is written: врачи́.

exercises.prompt: After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, щ, which plural ending is written?
exercises.explanation: This is the spelling rule: ы is replaced by и after those seven letters.

lessons.title: 9. Whose? and plural possessives
lessons.subtitle: Чей, чья, чьё, чьи, and мои́, твои́, на́ши, ва́ши

explanations.title: Possessives in the plural
explanations.body: Possessives agree with their noun in gender and in number. In the plural there is one form for all three genders: мои́ books, мои́ windows, мои́ brothers. The question word Whose? works the same way, so the form of чей tells you what kind of noun is coming.

tables.note: Его́ (his), её (her) and их (their) never change, in the plural either.

examples.text: Чей э́то дом? — Э́то мой дом.
examples.translation: Whose house is this? — It's my house.

examples.text: Чья э́то газе́та? — Э́то ва́ша газе́та.
examples.translation: Whose newspaper is this? — It's your newspaper.

examples.text: Чьё э́то окно́? — Э́то на́ше окно́.
examples.translation: Whose window is this? — It's our window.

examples.text: Чьи э́то кни́ги? — Э́то мои́ кни́ги.
examples.translation: Whose books are these? — They're my books.

exercises.promptTranslation: Whose house is this?
Whose book is this?
Whose window is this?
Whose children are these?

exercises.explanation: Plural noun, so the plural form мои́.
exercises.promptTranslation: These are my books.
Here are your glasses. (familiar)
Are your (polite) parents at home?

exercises.explanation: Его́ means “his” and never changes: его́ друзья́.
exercises.promptTranslation: These are his friends.

exercises.prompt: How many plural forms does мой have?

lessons.title: 10. Numbers 0–10
lessons.subtitle: Counting, and the genders of one and two

explanations.title: Zero to ten
explanations.body: These eleven words are the foundation for telling time, giving phone numbers and paying. Tap a number to hear it.

explanations.title: One and two have genders
explanations.body: Оди́н, одна́, одно́ agree with the noun. Two has two forms: два goes with masculine and neuter nouns, две with feminine ones. The noun after два, три and четы́ре changes its form too. You will see why later, so for now just choose the right number and copy the pairs.

examples.translation: There is only one student here.
There is only one book here.
There is only one window here.
There are two students here.
There are two books here.
There are two windows here.

explanations.title: A number after the noun
explanations.body: When a number comes after the noun as a label (a room number, a page, a bus), it never changes for gender.

examples.translation: number one
number two
number three

exercises.promptTranslation: There is only one student here.
There is only one book here.
There is only one window here.

exercises.explanation: Two takes the feminine form with a feminine noun.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are two books here.

exercises.explanation: Два goes with masculine and neuter nouns.
exercises.promptTranslation: There are two windows here.

exercises.prompt: Which of these numbers changes with the gender of the noun?
exercises.explanation: Of these, only one: оди́н, одна́, одно́. (Two also does: два, две.)

exercises.prompt: How do you say “number two” as a label?
exercises.explanation: After the noun the number doesn't change. Два но́мера would mean “two numbers”.

lessons.title: 11. Irregular plurals
lessons.subtitle: Words you have to learn as pairs

explanations.title: Plurals in -а or -я, with the stress on the ending
explanations.body: Some masculine nouns take -а (or -я after a soft stem) instead of -ы. The stress lands on that ending. There is no rule for which nouns do this: learn each one as a pair.

explanations.title: -ья, and plurals that look nothing like the singular
explanations.body: Some nouns take -ья. A few have a completely different plural, and a few change a letter. All of them have to be memorised.

tables.note: Отцы́ loses the е of оте́ц. Жёны and сёстры change е to ё.

explanations.title: Plural only
explanations.body: A few nouns exist only in the plural. Things that come as a pair or a set are the usual ones. You say мои́ очки́ (my glasses) and never use a singular.

examples.translation: Here are my glasses.
Where is your watch?

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of го́род?
exercises.explanation: Some masculine nouns take -а with the stress on it: города́.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of друг?
exercises.explanation: Друг takes -ья and г changes to з: друзья́.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of ребёнок?
exercises.explanation: Ребёнок (child) has a different plural: де́ти.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of челове́к?
exercises.explanation: Челове́к (person) has a different plural: лю́ди.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of мать?
exercises.explanation: Мать → ма́тери. Дочь → до́чери follows the same pattern.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of брат?
What is the plural of сестра́?
exercises.explanation: The е becomes ё in the plural: сёстры.

exercises.prompt: What is the plural of оте́ц?
What is the plural of сын?
Which of these nouns has no singular?
exercises.explanation: Очки́ (glasses) exists only in the plural, like часы́ and де́ньги.

lessons.title: 12. Patronymics
lessons.subtitle: Иван Петрович, Мария Павловна: the polite way to address adults

explanations.title: First name and patronymic
explanations.body: Adults you aren't close to are normally addressed by first name and patronymic (о́тчество): a middle name made from the father's first name. Никола́й Ива́нович means Nikolai, son of Ivan. Мари́я Па́вловна is Maria, daughter of Pavel. Use it, with вы, for a teacher, a boss, a colleague or anyone older. A patronymic has a masculine and a feminine form, so it follows the person's sex.

examples.translation: Hello, Maria Pavlovna!
This is Nikolai Ivanovich.

explanations.title: Forming the patronymic
explanations.body: Take the father's first name and add a suffix, which depends on how his name ends. Watch the fleeting vowel: Па́вел loses its е.

rows: Ники́та → Ники́тич / Ники́тична · Илья́ → Ильи́ч / Ильи́нична
tables.note: A few names are irregular, for example Дми́трий → Дми́триевич.

exercises.explanation: A daughter takes -овна after a name ending in a consonant.
exercises.promptTranslation: Anna, daughter of Ivan.

exercises.explanation: Names in -й take -евич for a son and -евна for a daughter.
exercises.promptTranslation: Boris, son of Sergei.

exercises.explanation: Па́вел loses its е before the suffix: Па́вловна.
exercises.promptTranslation: Olga, daughter of Pavel.

exercises.explanation: Names in -а take -ич for a son and -ична for a daughter.
exercises.promptTranslation: Alexei, son of Nikita.

exercises.prompt: How do you politely address your teacher Мари́я Па́вловна?
exercises.explanation: First name, then patronymic, with вы.

exercises.prompt: What is the first name of the father of Никола́й Ива́нович?
exercises.explanation: The patronymic is built from the father's first name.

exercises.prompt: Which of these patronymics belongs to a man?
exercises.explanation: -ич endings (-ович, -евич, -ьевич) are masculine; -на endings are feminine.

exercises.prompt: Whom do you normally address by first name and patronymic?
options: An adult you aren't close to, such as a teacher or a colleague
exercises.explanation: It is respectful and slightly formal. Friends and family use the first name alone.

units.title: Unit 3: Describing, locating and verbs

lessons.title: 13. Adjectives agree with their noun
lessons.subtitle: Но́вый дом, но́вая кни́га, но́вое окно́, но́вые кни́ги

explanations.title: Gender and number
explanations.body: An adjective describes a noun, and it takes that noun's gender and number. The question words show the four forms: Како́й? (masculine), Кака́я? (feminine), Како́е? (neuter), Каки́е? (plural). The ending tells you which noun it belongs to. Later it will also match the noun's case.

explanations.title: Before the noun, or after it
explanations.body: An adjective can stand before its noun (но́вый дом) or describe it afterwards, with no verb in between (Дом но́вый). Either way it matches the noun.

examples.translation: a new house
a new book
a new window
new books
The house is old.
The book is old.

exercises.promptTranslation: This is a new house.
This is a new book.
This is a new window.
These are new books.

exercises.explanation: Дом is masculine, so the description is too.
exercises.promptTranslation: The house is old.
The car is new.
The letter is interesting.

exercises.explanation: Журна́лы is plural, whatever the gender of журна́л.
exercises.promptTranslation: The magazines are interesting.

exercises.prompt: Which question word goes with a feminine noun?
exercises.explanation: Како́й is masculine, кака́я feminine, како́е neuter, каки́е plural.

lessons.title: 14. Adjective endings: soft stems, spelling, stress
lessons.subtitle: Си́ний, ру́сский, хоро́ший, большо́й

explanations.title: Three groups change the ending
explanations.body: Most adjectives are like но́вый. Three groups differ. A soft stem (си́ний, blue) takes -ий, -яя, -ее, -ие. After г, к, х the masculine is -ий, not -ый, and the plural -ие: this is the spelling rule you met with plurals. After ж, ш, ч, щ the same happens, and an unstressed neuter ending is -ее, not -ое. Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: When the ending is stressed
explanations.body: If the stress falls on the ending, the masculine ends in -о́й instead of -ый or -ий, and the other forms are -а́я, -о́е, -ы́е. After к and ш the plural is still -и́е, by the spelling rule. The words большо́й, како́й and молодо́й are all in this group.

exercises.explanation: Дом is masculine, and the stress is on the ending: большо́й.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a big house.
This is a big school.

exercises.explanation: Окно́ is neuter. After к the ending is still -ое when unstressed.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a small window.
These are small children.
This is a Russian book.

exercises.explanation: After ш an unstressed neuter ending is -ее.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a good window.

exercises.explanation: Мо́ре is neuter, and a soft stem gives -ее.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a blue sea.

exercises.explanation: Челове́к is masculine, and the ending is stressed: молодо́й.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a young man.

exercises.prompt: Why is it хоро́шее and not хоро́шое?
options: Because хоро́ший is a plural form
Because the stress is on the ending
After ж, ш, ч, щ an unstressed neuter ending is -ее
It is an exception with no rule
exercises.explanation: It is a spelling rule. When the ending is stressed it stays -ое, as in большо́е.

exercises.prompt: Which masculine ending shows that the stress is on the ending?

lessons.title: 15. Ordinal numbers
lessons.subtitle: Пе́рвый, второ́й, тре́тий…

explanations.title: First, second, third
explanations.body: Ordinal numbers are adjectives: they agree with their noun in gender and number, and later in case. Most behave like но́вый. Второ́й has a stressed ending. Тре́тий is a soft adjective with its own forms.

examples.translation: the first lesson
the second book
the third word
the first lessons

explanations.title: Fourth to tenth
explanations.body: From four on, the ordinals are formed from the number. Four of them end in a stressed -о́й (второ́й, шесто́й, седьмо́й, восьмо́й) and take -а́я, -о́е, -ы́е. The others behave like но́вый.

exercises.promptTranslation: This is the first lesson.

exercises.explanation: Кни́га is feminine, and the stress is on the ending.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is the second book.

exercises.explanation: Сло́во is neuter, and тре́тий has the soft forms тре́тья, тре́тье, тре́тьи.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is the third word.
These are the first lessons.
This is the sixth room.

exercises.prompt: What is the feminine form of тре́тий?
exercises.explanation: Тре́тий is a soft adjective with its own forms: тре́тья, тре́тье, тре́тьи.

lessons.title: 16. Where? The prepositional case
lessons.subtitle: В журна́ле, на окне́, в тетра́ди: the ending that says “where”

explanations.title: Saying where something is
explanations.body: To say where something is, Russian uses the prepositional case. It answers Где? and always follows a preposition. For now, that means в (in) or на (on, at). The noun changes its ending: most take -е, and nouns in -ь, -ий, -ия, -ие take -и. Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: Where, not where to
explanations.body: This case answers Где? (where is it?), not Куда́? (where is it going?). The stress often moves onto the ending (слова́рь → в словаре́, окно́ → на окне́). The prepositional is used only after a preposition, which is why it carries that name.

examples.translation: Mom is at school.
The children are in the room.
Dad is at work.
They are in town.

exercises.promptTranslation: Mom is at school.
The children are in the room.
Dad is at work.

exercises.explanation: A masculine noun ending in a consonant takes -е.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are in town.

exercises.explanation: A masculine noun ending in a consonant takes -е.
exercises.promptTranslation: Dad is at the bank.
They are in the museum.
The pen is in the notebook.
We are in the building.

exercises.explanation: Neuter -е stays -е, so here the prepositional looks like the nominative.
exercises.promptTranslation: They are at the sea.

exercises.prompt: Which question does the prepositional case answer here?
exercises.explanation: It states location. Where something is going uses a different case, which comes later.

lessons.title: 17. В or на?
lessons.subtitle: Which preposition goes with which place

explanations.title: The general idea
explanations.body: В (in) goes with enclosed spaces that have clear borders: rooms, buildings, towns, countries. На (on, at) goes with surfaces, open areas and events. Both take the prepositional case when they answer Где? Tap a row to hear it.

explanations.title: Pairs to memorise
explanations.body: Some places do not follow the logic, and you just have to learn the pair. These are common ones that take на.

tables.note: Before some consonant clusters в becomes во: во дворе́ (in the yard).

exercises.explanation: A school is an enclosed space: в.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are at school.

exercises.explanation: A table is a surface: на.
exercises.promptTranslation: The book is on the table.

exercises.explanation: Ку́хня is one of the pairs to learn: на ку́хне.
exercises.promptTranslation: Mom is in the kitchen.

exercises.explanation: На рабо́те is a fixed pair.
exercises.promptTranslation: Dad is at work.
The children are outside.

exercises.explanation: A bank is a building: в.
exercises.promptTranslation: He is at the bank.
We are in class.

exercises.explanation: A hospital is a building: в.
exercises.promptTranslation: She is in the hospital.

exercises.explanation: На по́чте is a fixed pair.
exercises.promptTranslation: I am at the post office.

exercises.explanation: Before some consonant clusters, в becomes во: во дворе́ (in the yard). На дворе́ also exists, but it is an idiom meaning “outdoors”, as in на дворе́ хо́лодно.
exercises.promptTranslation: They are in the yard.

lessons.title: 18. This and that: э́тот, тот, and э́то
lessons.subtitle: Demonstratives agree with the noun; э́то never does

explanations.title: Э́тот and тот
explanations.body: Э́тот points at something close, or just mentioned. Тот points at something farther away, or mentioned earlier. Like adjectives, they agree with the noun in gender and number.

examples.text: Э́тот стол большо́й, а тот ма́ленький.
examples.translation: This table is big, and that one is small.

examples.text: Э́та кни́га но́вая, а та ста́рая.
examples.translation: This book is new, and that one is old.

examples.text: Э́ти дома́ но́вые, а те ста́рые.
examples.translation: These houses are new, and those are old.

explanations.title: Э́то is a different word
explanations.body: Don't confuse the demonstratives with э́то meaning “this is”. That word has one form and never changes. A demonstrative goes before a noun and agrees with it, so on its own “э́та кни́га” is only the phrase “this book”, not a sentence. The neuter э́то looks identical to the fixed э́то, so there context decides.

rows: Э́то кни́га. = This is a book.
Э́та кни́га но́вая. = This book is new.

exercises.promptTranslation: This house is old.
This book is new.

exercises.explanation: Masculine, and “that one” far away: тот.
exercises.promptTranslation: This table is big, and that one is small.
This book is new, and that one is old.
These houses are new, and those are old.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “This is a book”?
exercises.explanation: Э́то + noun is a full sentence. Э́та кни́га is only “this book”.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “These children are at home”?
exercises.explanation: Э́ти agrees with the plural noun and means “these”. Э́то де́ти… would be “these are children…”.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is a fixed word that never changes?
exercises.explanation: Э́то (“this is”) has one form. Don't confuse it with the neuter of э́тот, which looks identical.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “that one” (masculine, far away)?
exercises.explanation: Тот, та, то, те: that / those.

lessons.title: 19. Was and were: the past of быть
lessons.subtitle: Four forms: был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли

explanations.title: Four forms
explanations.body: In the present tense быть disappears. In the past it comes back, and Russian needs four forms where English has two (was, were): three for the singular genders and one for the plural. You choose by the subject. Я and ты take был or была́ depending on who is speaking: a woman says я была́. Вы always takes бы́ли, even for one polite person.

rows: Вчера́ он был до́ма. = Yesterday he was at home.
Вчера́ она́ была́ до́ма. = Yesterday she was at home.
Письмо́ бы́ло на столе́. = The letter was on the table.
Вчера́ мы бы́ли в шко́ле. = Yesterday we were at school.

explanations.title: Кто, что, and the negative
explanations.body: Кто (who) always takes the masculine singular, even when the answer is a woman. Что (what) always takes the neuter. When быть is negated, the stress jumps onto не in every form except the feminine.

examples.text: Кто был до́ма? — До́ма была́ моя́ сестра́.
examples.translation: Who was at home? — My sister was at home.

examples.text: Что бы́ло на столе́? — На столе́ бы́ли де́ньги.
examples.translation: What was on the table? — There was money on the table.

exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday mom was at home.
Yesterday my brother was at work.
Yesterday the children were at school.

exercises.explanation: The speaker is a woman, so the feminine form.
exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday I was at home. (a woman speaking)

exercises.explanation: Вы always takes the plural form, even for one polite person.
exercises.promptTranslation: Were you at home yesterday? (one person, polite)
What was on the table?

exercises.explanation: Кто takes the masculine, even if the answer turns out to be a woman.
exercises.promptTranslation: Who was here?

exercises.prompt: Which negated form keeps the stress on the verb?
exercises.explanation: Only the feminine keeps the stress on the verb: не была́.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “The letter wasn't there”?
exercises.explanation: Письмо́ is neuter, so бы́ло, with the stress on не.

exercises.prompt: A man says “Вчера́ я был на рабо́те.” How does a woman say it?
exercises.explanation: The verb follows the speaker's gender.

lessons.title: 20. The present tense: your first verbs
lessons.subtitle: Жить and рабо́тать: each person has its own ending

explanations.title: Infinitive and endings
explanations.body: The dictionary form of a verb is the infinitive, usually ending in -ть: жить (to live), рабо́тать (to work). In the present tense each person has its own ending, so Russian often needs no pronoun. Changing the endings like this is called conjugating. These two are called first-conjugation verbs. Tap a row to hear it.

tables.note: The stem of жить changes (жи- becomes жив-), so learn it as it is.

explanations.title: Putting it together
explanations.body: You can now build real sentences: в or на with the prepositional case for the place, and не before the verb to negate it. There is also only one present tense: Я рабо́таю covers both “I work” and “I am working”.

examples.translation: I live in a house.
Mom works at a school.
Where do you live?
They don't work here.

exercises.promptTranslation: I work at a school.
Do you live here?

exercises.explanation: Он, она́ and a singular noun take -ет.
exercises.promptTranslation: Mom works at a bank.
We live in a house.
They work at the post office.
Do you live in town? (polite or plural)

exercises.prompt: How do you say “He doesn't work here”?
exercises.explanation: Не goes right before the verb.

exercises.prompt: What does “Я рабо́таю” cover in English?
exercises.explanation: Russian has a single present tense.

units.title: Unit 4: More verbs

lessons.title: 21. Verbs in -ать: one pattern, many verbs
lessons.subtitle: Чита́ю, де́лаю, зна́ю, понима́ю

explanations.title: Drop -ть, add the ending
explanations.body: You already conjugated жить and рабо́тать. Most verbs ending in -ать work the same way. Take off -ть to get the stem, then add the ending that matches the subject: -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют. For these verbs the stress never moves, so it is the same syllable in every form. Tap a row to hear it.

tables.note: to read · to do, to make · to know · to understand

explanations.title: No “do” in Russian
explanations.body: English needs a helper verb for questions and negatives (Do you know? I don't know). Russian does not: the verb alone is enough, and a question is just the same sentence said with a rising voice. Де́лать is only for really doing or making something, so Что ты де́лаешь? means “What are you doing?”, never the helper “do”.

examples.translation: Do you know?
I don't know.
What are you doing?
They read a lot.
Do you understand?
I think this is good.

exercises.promptTranslation: I know that you are at home.
Do you understand well?
What is he doing?
We read a lot.
Do you know this?
What do you think?

exercises.prompt: Which ending does ты take with these verbs?
How do you say “I don't understand”?
exercises.explanation: Не goes right before the verb.

exercises.prompt: How do you ask “What do you do?” (to one friend)?
exercises.explanation: No helper verb: just Что + ты + the ты-form.

lessons.title: 22. Verbs that change their stem
lessons.subtitle: Пишу́, пи́шешь: learn these one by one

explanations.title: Same endings, different stem
explanations.body: A few verbs do not keep their infinitive stem. Писа́ть (to write) loses its -а- and its с becomes ш: пиш-. Ждать (to wait) loses its -а-: жд-. The endings are the ones you know. When the ending carries the stress, -е- is written as -ё- (ждёшь, like живёшь). Whatever changes shows up in every form, so learn the я-form together with the infinitive.

tables.note: to write · to wait · to live. Note -у and -ут after a consonant (not -ю and -ют).

explanations.title: Where the stress goes
explanations.body: Писа́ть keeps its stress on the stem in every form except я, where it jumps to the ending: пишу́. Ждать and жить have the stress on the ending throughout. Both patterns are common, so listen for the stress each time you tap a form.

examples.translation: I'm writing a letter.
Do you write often?
We're waiting at home.
They're waiting here.

exercises.promptTranslation: I'm writing a letter.

exercises.explanation: Ты takes -ешь, and the stress stays on the stem.
exercises.promptTranslation: Are you writing a letter?
We're writing a dialogue.

exercises.explanation: Они́ takes -ут: the stem ends in a consonant.
exercises.promptTranslation: They write often.

exercises.explanation: Мы takes -ём here, because the ending is stressed.
exercises.promptTranslation: We're waiting here.

exercises.explanation: The я-form of ждать is жду.
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm waiting for you at home.
They live here.

exercises.prompt: What happens to the stem of писа́ть in the present tense?
options: Part of it drops out and the consonant changes
exercises.explanation: Пиш- replaces писа-, and the change appears in every form.

lessons.title: 23. The second family: говори́ть, учи́ть, смотре́ть
lessons.subtitle: Говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т

explanations.title: Drop -ть and the vowel before it
explanations.body: Russian has two families of verbs. You have met the first (-ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют). The second family has its own endings: -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят. To conjugate one, drop -ть and the vowel before it (говори́-ть → говор-), then add the ending.

tables.note: to speak · to learn, to teach · to watch, to look. Why -у and -ат in учи́ть? See lesson 25.

explanations.title: Which family is a verb in?
explanations.body: Almost every verb in -ить belongs to the second family. A handful of others do too, including смотре́ть, ви́деть and слы́шать (to hear). Most verbs in -ать and -ять belong to the first. When you learn a new verb, learn its я-form and ты-form with it, and the family is obvious: -ешь means first, -ишь means second.

examples.translation: We speak Russian.
He learns words well.
Are you watching a film?
They hear well.

exercises.promptTranslation: I speak Russian.
Do you speak English?
She is watching a film.
We are learning new words.
Do you hear me?
They speak Russian.

exercises.prompt: Which ending belongs to the second family?
exercises.explanation: Ты takes -ишь in the second family and -ешь in the first.

exercises.prompt: Which verb belongs to the second family?
exercises.explanation: Almost all verbs in -ить are second family.

exercises.prompt: What do you drop from смотре́ть before adding an ending?

lessons.title: 24. When the я-form changes its consonant
lessons.subtitle: Ви́жу, ви́дишь: only the first person changes

explanations.title: One form that is different
explanations.body: Many second-family verbs change the last consonant of the stem, but only in the я-form. The other five forms use the consonant you see in the infinitive. Видеть is the model: д becomes ж in ви́жу, then it is back to д in ви́дишь, ви́дит, ви́дим, ви́дите, ви́дят.

tables.note: to see · to love, to like

explanations.title: Common changes
explanations.body: The change is not random: the same few swaps keep coming back. You have to learn which verbs do it, but the я-form shows you straight away. Смотре́ть, говори́ть and учи́ть do not change at all, so compare them with the verbs below.

exercises.explanation: In the я-form д becomes ж.
exercises.promptTranslation: I see a house.

exercises.explanation: Only the я-form changes. Ты has the plain д.
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you see me?
We see the school.

exercises.explanation: The я-form is люблю́ (б becomes бл).
exercises.promptTranslation: I love this book.

exercises.explanation: Они́ takes -ят, with the plain б.
exercises.promptTranslation: They love rock music.

exercises.explanation: Ходи́ть: д becomes ж in the я-form.
exercises.promptTranslation: I often walk in the park.

exercises.explanation: Only the я-form changes: мы has the plain д.
exercises.promptTranslation: We are sitting at home.

exercises.prompt: In which form does the consonant change?
exercises.explanation: The change affects the я-form only.

exercises.prompt: What is the я-form of плати́ть?

lessons.title: 25. Two spelling rules
lessons.subtitle: Which letters you may not write after others

explanations.title: The seven-letter rule
explanations.body: After the seven letters к, г, х, ж, ч, ш, щ, Russian never writes ы, я or ю. It writes и, а, у instead. That is why the plural of кни́га is кни́ги (never кни́гы), why the они́-form of учи́ть is у́чат (never у́чят), and why the я-form of писа́ть is пишу́ (never пишю́). Whenever a regular ending would put one of those letters after these consonants, the spelling changes, and the sound stays the same.

headers: After к г х ж ч ш щ

explanations.title: The five-letter rule
explanations.body: After ж, ч, ш, щ and ц, an unstressed о is written е. You see it in neuter adjectives and in some pronouns: хоро́шее (not хоро́шое), на́ше (not на́шо). If the о is stressed, it stays: большо́е.

tables.note: The five-letter rule applies after ж ч ш щ ц; the seven-letter rule after к г х ж ч ш щ.

examples.translation: This is good wine.
This is our window.
They are learning words.
I'm writing a letter.

exercises.explanation: After г you write и, never ы.
exercises.promptTranslation: Here are my books.

exercises.explanation: After к you write и, never ы.
exercises.promptTranslation: Here are your pens.

exercises.explanation: After ч you write а, never я.
exercises.promptTranslation: They learn words.

exercises.explanation: After ш you write у, never ю.
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm writing a letter.

exercises.explanation: Хоро́шее is neuter, so a neuter noun follows. Note ее after ш.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is good wine.

exercises.explanation: After ш an unstressed о becomes е: на́ше.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is our window.

exercises.explanation: After к and г you cannot write ы.

exercises.prompt: Which of these letters does the five-letter rule NOT include?
exercises.explanation: The five letters are ж, ч, ш, щ, ц. К belongs to the seven-letter rule only.

exercises.prompt: Why is it большо́е окно́, not большее?
options: The о is stressed, so it stays
Because ш is a soft letter
It is an exception with no reason
exercises.explanation: Only an unstressed о changes to е.

lessons.title: 26. Commands: Чита́й! Пиши́!
lessons.subtitle: Making the imperative from the они́-form

explanations.title: How to build a command
explanations.body: Take the они́-form of the verb and drop the ending (-ут, -ют, -ат, -ят). If a vowel is left at the end, add -й (to one friend, ты) or -йте (to someone you address as вы, or to several people). If a consonant is left, add -и (ты) or -и́те (вы), and the stress goes on the и in all the verbs below. Add пожа́луйста to be polite.

tables.note: Stress of -и commands lands on the и, as shown.

explanations.title: In use
explanations.body: A command is addressed to someone, so ты or вы is already understood. Use the вы-form with people you do not know well, a group, or anyone you would address politely. To tell someone not to do something, put не before the command: Не чита́й!

examples.translation: Read, please! (to a friend)
Write to me! (to a friend)
Listen to me! (to a group, or politely)
Please answer. (polite)
Don't ask!

exercises.promptTranslation: Read, please!
Listen to me!

exercises.explanation: Пи́шут → пиш- (a consonant), so add -и, stressed.
exercises.promptTranslation: Write to me!

exercises.explanation: A consonant stem plus -ите for вы.
exercises.promptTranslation: Please write to me.
Speak Russian!
Answer the question!

exercises.prompt: What do you add to a stem that ends in a vowel (to one friend)?
How do you say “Don't read!” to a friend?
Which command is polite or plural?

units.title: Unit 5: The accusative, days and numbers

lessons.title: 27. The accusative: the thing you read, write or see
lessons.subtitle: Я чита́ю кни́гу, Я ви́жу шко́лу

explanations.title: The direct object
explanations.body: The direct object is whatever the action lands on: what you read, write, see, know. In Russian it goes into the accusative case and answers Что? (what?) or Кого́? (whom?). Nothing goes before it. For things (not people or animals) most nouns do not change at all. Only feminine nouns in -а and -я change: -а becomes -у and -я becomes -ю.

tables.note: Plural things don't change either: Я чита́ю журна́лы.

examples.translation: I'm reading a magazine.
He's writing a letter.
We see the school.
Are you reading a newspaper?
I see a door.

explanations.title: A stress shift to watch
explanations.body: In some feminine nouns the stress is on the ending in the nominative and jumps to the stem in the accusative. These are very common words, so listen for it.

tables.note: board · wall · hand · mountain · head

exercises.promptTranslation: I'm reading a book.

exercises.explanation: A neuter thing doesn't change in the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: He's writing a letter.
We see the school.
I'm reading a newspaper.

exercises.explanation: A masculine thing doesn't change in the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: We're watching a film.
I see a door.

exercises.explanation: Стена́ becomes сте́ну: the stress jumps to the stem.
exercises.promptTranslation: I see the wall.

exercises.prompt: Which noun does not change in the accusative?
exercises.explanation: Only feminine nouns in -а and -я change.

exercises.prompt: Which ending marks a feminine noun in -я as a direct object?

exercises.explanation: A direct object is accusative: кни́га → кни́гу.

lessons.title: 28. The accusative with people and animals
lessons.subtitle: Я ви́жу студе́нта, Я зна́ю учи́теля

explanations.title: Masculine people and animals take an ending
explanations.body: For a masculine noun that is a person or an animal, the accusative is not the same as the nominative. After a hard consonant add -а. If the noun ends in -ь or -й, replace that letter with -я. Nouns in -ец lose their -е-, as in the plural: оте́ц becomes отца́.

examples.translation: I see the student.
He knows the teacher.
Do you know Nikolai?
We see [my] father.

explanations.title: Women, and men whose names end in -а or -я
explanations.body: Women are easy: whether a feminine noun is a person or a thing makes no difference. Девушка becomes де́вушку, Та́ня becomes Та́ню, and мать stays мать. Men with nouns in -а or -я, such as па́па and дя́дя, decline like feminine nouns, so they take -у and -ю.

exercises.promptTranslation: I see the student.
We know the teacher.
Do you see [my] father?
We know Nikolai.

exercises.explanation: Па́па ends in -а, so it takes -у like a feminine noun.
exercises.promptTranslation: I see dad.
He knows Tanya.
We see [our] uncle.

exercises.explanation: A woman takes -у like any feminine noun in -а.
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you know this girl?

exercises.prompt: Which noun changes in the accusative?
exercises.explanation: A masculine person takes an ending; masculine things don't.

lessons.title: 29. Pronouns in the accusative: me, you, him, her
lessons.subtitle: Меня́, тебя́, его́, её, нас, вас, их

explanations.title: Seven new forms
explanations.body: Personal pronouns have their own accusative forms. Learn them as a set: they are used all the time (Я зна́ю тебя́, Он ви́дит нас).

explanations.title: The extra н after a preposition
explanations.body: When его́, её or их comes right after a preposition, a н is added at the front: него́, неё, них. Without a preposition there is no н. The same words are also the possessives “his, her, their” (его́ дом, её кни́га, их маши́на), and those never take н.

examples.translation: I live in his house. (possessive: no н)
He is looking at me. (меня́ never changes)

exercises.explanation: Direct object: accusative of я is меня́.
exercises.promptTranslation: He sees me.
I see you.
We know her.

exercises.explanation: After the preposition на, её becomes неё.
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm looking at her.
Do you hear us?
We see them.

exercises.explanation: After a preposition его́ becomes него́.
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm looking at him.

exercises.explanation: Here его́ means “his”, a possessive, so no н.
exercises.promptTranslation: I live in his house.

exercises.prompt: Which word means “you” (one friend) as a direct object?
Why do we say на неё but Я зна́ю её?
options: A preposition adds н- before его́, её and их

lessons.title: 30. Adjectives in the accusative
lessons.subtitle: Но́вую кни́гу, но́вого студе́нта

explanations.title: Adjectives follow the noun
explanations.body: The adjective takes the same case as its noun. So when the noun is a direct object, the adjective must be accusative too. Where the noun does not change (masculine things, neuter, plural things), the adjective does not change either. A feminine noun takes -ую (hard stem) or -юю (soft stem).

explanations.title: Masculine people: -ого and -его
explanations.body: With a masculine person or animal both the noun and the adjective change. A hard adjective ends in -ого, a soft one in -его. Spelling rules still apply: after к, г, х you keep the hard ending (ру́сского), and after ж, ч, ш, щ an unstressed о turns into е (хоро́шего). A stressed о stays (большо́го).

rows: after к the ending is hard
five-letter rule: о becomes е after ш

examples.translation: I know the new student.
We know a good teacher.
He sees a big cat.
Do you know the Russian student?

exercises.promptTranslation: I'm reading a new book.

exercises.explanation: A masculine thing keeps its nominative form.
exercises.promptTranslation: We see a new house.

exercises.explanation: A neuter keeps its nominative form.
exercises.promptTranslation: I see a big window.
I know the new student.

exercises.explanation: After ш an unstressed о is written е.
exercises.promptTranslation: We know a good teacher.

exercises.explanation: After к the ending stays hard: -ого.
exercises.promptTranslation: He knows the Russian student.

exercises.explanation: The о is stressed, so it stays: -ого.
exercises.promptTranslation: I see a big cat.

exercises.explanation: Plural things keep their nominative form.
exercises.promptTranslation: We read interesting magazines.

exercises.prompt: Which adjective endings go with a feminine direct object?

options: After ш an unstressed о is written е

lessons.title: 31. My, this, which: other words that agree
lessons.subtitle: Мою́ сестру́, э́того бра́та, каку́ю кни́гу?

explanations.title: They decline like adjectives
explanations.body: Many words that go with a noun behave like adjectives: мой, твой, наш, ваш (my, your, our, your), э́тот and тот (this, that), како́й (which), чей (whose), and the ordinal numbers пе́рвый, второ́й, тре́тий. In the accusative they follow the same three rules: no change for things, -ого or -его for masculine people, and a feminine ending for feminine nouns.

tables.note: Neuter and plural things: no change. Его́, её, их never change at all.

explanations.title: In sentences
explanations.body: Your choice depends on the noun that follows: its gender, and whether it is a person. Мой and твой take the soft endings (моего́, мою́). Чей and тре́тий also keep a soft sign in every form except the masculine thing: чью, чьего́, тре́тью, тре́тьего. Наш and ваш follow the spelling rule you met in lesson 25: на́шего, ва́шего.

examples.translation: Do you know my brother?
I see my sister.
We know this student.
Which book are you reading?
I'm reading the first page.
Whose car do you see?

exercises.promptTranslation: I see my sister.
Do you know my brother?
We know this student.
I see this girl.
Which book are you reading?
We see our mom.

exercises.prompt: Which form is used with мой and a masculine thing, like дом?
What is the accusative of тре́тья for a feminine object?
exercises.explanation: Third is a soft-stem word, so -ю.

exercises.prompt: Which words never change for case?

lessons.title: 32. On Monday, on Tuesday: the days of the week
lessons.subtitle: В понеде́льник, во вто́рник, в сре́ду

explanations.title: The week
explanations.body: The days are not capitalised in Russian. To say “on Monday” use в plus the accusative, and the question is Когда́? (when?). In во вто́рник the preposition becomes во because the next word starts with two consonants. Masculine and neuter days do not change; the feminine days (среда́, пя́тница, суббо́та) take -у, and сре́ду moves its stress.

explanations.title: In use
explanations.body: Use the nominative to say what day it is today or tomorrow, and в + accusative for when something happens. This is the same accusative you have been learning: it just follows в.

examples.translation: Today is Monday.
Tomorrow is Tuesday.
On Wednesday I'm at home.
On Tuesday we work.
On Saturday we don't work.

exercises.explanation: Days take в plus the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: On Monday I work.

exercises.explanation: Before вто́рник the preposition is во.
exercises.promptTranslation: On Tuesday we're at home.

exercises.explanation: Feminine day: -а becomes -у, and the stress jumps to the stem.
exercises.promptTranslation: On Wednesday I'm at home.
On Friday we watch a film.
On Saturday I don't work.

exercises.explanation: To say what day it is, use the nominative.
exercises.promptTranslation: Today is Thursday.

exercises.prompt: Which question do these phrases answer?
Which day takes во, not в?
exercises.explanation: Во before two consonants: во вто́рник.

lessons.title: 33. Eleven to twenty
lessons.subtitle: Оди́ннадцать, двена́дцать … два́дцать

explanations.title: The teens
explanations.body: The numbers 11 to 19 are built from the unit plus -на-дцать, which literally means “on ten”. They all end in a soft sign, and the unit's own soft sign disappears (пять → пятна́дцать). Twenty is its own word. Ordinals are made by swapping -ь for -ый: двена́дцать → двена́дцатый. They behave like any adjective, so they agree with their noun.

examples.translation: Today is the twelfth day.
This is the fifteenth room.
Today is the nineteenth day.

exercises.promptTranslation: Five and ten is fifteen.
Nine and ten is nineteen.
Two and ten is twelve.

exercises.explanation: Урок is masculine, so the ordinal takes -ый.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is the thirteenth lesson.
This is the twentieth room.

exercises.prompt: What do the numbers 11 to 19 have in common?
How do the ordinals from 11 to 20 behave?
options: Like adjectives: they agree with the noun

exercises.explanation: Ко́мната is feminine, so the ordinal ends in -ая.

units.title: Unit 6: Past tense, places and everyday sentences

lessons.title: 34. The past tense of verbs
lessons.subtitle: Чита́л, чита́ла, чита́ло, чита́ли

explanations.title: Drop -ть, add -л
explanations.body: To make the past tense, take the infinitive, drop -ть, and add -л plus an ending for the gender or number of the subject: nothing for masculine, -а for feminine, -о for neuter, -и for plural. You have already seen this pattern in был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли. Tap a row to hear it.

tables.note: In the past the verb shows only gender and number, never the person.

explanations.title: Gender and number only
explanations.body: In the present tense the verb shows the person (я чита́ю, ты чита́ешь). In the past it shows only gender and number, exactly like быть. So я, ты and он, all masculine, use the same form. A woman says я чита́ла, and вы always takes the plural, even for one polite person. Irregular present stems do not matter: писа́ть gives писа́л, not пиша́л.

examples.translation: Yesterday I read a magazine. (a man speaking)
Yesterday I read a magazine. (a woman speaking)
She was writing a letter.
We saw this film.
Did you speak Russian? (polite)

exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday I read a book. (a man speaking)
Yesterday she wrote a letter.
Yesterday we saw a film.
Yesterday I wrote a letter. (a woman speaking)
Did you speak Russian yesterday? (one person, polite)

exercises.explanation: A direct object: feminine in -а takes -у.
exercises.promptTranslation: The children listened to music.
They lived here for a long time.

exercises.prompt: What do you drop from an infinitive to make the past tense?
exercises.explanation: Чита́ть → чита́-, then add -л and the ending.

exercises.prompt: A woman says “I was reading a book.” Which is correct?
exercises.explanation: The verb follows the speaker's gender.

exercises.prompt: In the past tense, what does the verb agree with?
exercises.explanation: That is why я, ты and он all take the same masculine form.

lessons.title: 35. Two aspects: the process and the result
lessons.subtitle: Писа́л / написа́л, покупа́л / купи́л

explanations.title: Most verbs come in pairs
explanations.body: Most Russian verbs have two partners, called aspects. The imperfective names the activity: it stresses the process, the duration or the repetition. The perfective names one finished action and its result. Almost every verb you have learned so far is imperfective. The perfective partner is usually the same verb with a prefix (писа́ть → написа́ть), though some pairs are different words (покупа́ть → купи́ть). Learn them as pairs.

explanations.title: Which one do I need?
explanations.body: In the past tense, ask yourself: am I describing the activity, or telling that it got done? Words like весь ве́чер (all evening), до́лго (for a long time), ча́сто (often) and ка́ждый день (every day) point to the imperfective. Words like наконе́ц (finally) and уже́ (already), or a single result you can show, point to the perfective. The perfective has no ordinary present tense, so for what is happening now you always use the imperfective.

examples.text: Вчера́ я весь ве́чер чита́л кни́гу.
examples.translation: Yesterday I read a book all evening. (process)
Yesterday I read this book through. (finished)
He wrote a letter for a long time. (process)
He finally wrote the letter! (result)

examples.text: Вот моя́ но́вая маши́на. Я купи́л её вчера́.
examples.translation: Here is my new car. I bought it yesterday.

exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday I wrote a letter all evening.

exercises.explanation: Наконе́ц points to a finished result: perfective.
exercises.promptTranslation: I finally wrote the letter!

exercises.prompt: Вот моя́ но́вая маши́на! Я ___ её вчера́.
exercises.explanation: One completed purchase with a result you can show.
exercises.promptTranslation: Here is my new car! I bought it yesterday.
She often read books.

exercises.explanation: Уже́ says it is already done: perfective.
exercises.promptTranslation: He has already done the lesson.

exercises.explanation: Asking about the activity itself: imperfective.
exercises.promptTranslation: What were you doing yesterday evening?

exercises.prompt: Which aspect tells of a finished result?
exercises.explanation: The perfective names a completed action.

exercises.prompt: Which verb is the perfective partner of покупа́ть?
Which sentence says you finished the book?
exercises.explanation: The perfective with a prefix names the result.

exercises.prompt: Which aspect do you use for what is happening right now?
exercises.explanation: The perfective has no ordinary present tense.

lessons.title: 36. Where at? Where to?
lessons.subtitle: Где? в шко́ле — Куда́? в шко́лу

explanations.title: Two questions, two cases
explanations.body: English says “where” for both rest and movement, and then adds a preposition. Russian has two question words and the case does the work. Где? (where at?) takes в or на with the prepositional case: the place where something is. Куда́? (where to?) takes в or на with the accusative: the place someone is heading for. Which preposition each noun takes (в or на) is the same for both questions.

tables.note: Nouns that never change (кафе́, кино́) look the same both ways: only the question tells you.

examples.translation: Where are you? — I'm at school.

examples.text: Куда́ ты идёшь? — Я иду́ в шко́лу.
examples.translation: Where are you going? — I'm going to school.
Mom is at the post office.
Mom is going to the post office.

explanations.title: Here, there, home
explanations.body: A few small words also come in two forms, one for each question. Learn them as pairs.

examples.translation: I'm at home.
I'm going home.

exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you? — I'm at school.

exercises.explanation: Куда́? needs the accusative: шко́ла → шко́лу.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you going? — I'm going to school.

exercises.explanation: По́чта takes на; where at → prepositional.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where is mom? — She's at the post office.
Where is he going? — He's going to the post office.

exercises.explanation: Стадио́н takes на; where at → prepositional.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are they? — They're at the stadium.

exercises.explanation: A masculine thing doesn't change in the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you going? — We're going to a lesson.

exercises.explanation: Домо́й is the “going home” word. До́ма means “at home”.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you going? — I'm going home.

exercises.prompt: Which question word asks about location?
exercises.explanation: Где? = where at? Куда́? = where to?
Motion toward a place takes the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says you are going to the library?

lessons.title: 37. Going on foot: идти́
lessons.subtitle: Иду́, идёшь, идёт

explanations.title: Идти́ in the present and past
explanations.body: Идти́ means to go on foot, in one direction. It is irregular but follows the first-conjugation pattern in the present. The past tense is also irregular: шёл, шла, шло, шли.

tables.note: Command: иди́! (to a friend), иди́те! (polite or to a group).

explanations.title: Where to?
explanations.body: Say where you are going with в or на and the accusative, or with a little word like домо́й, туда́ or сюда́. People also use идти́ for events in town: you go to a concert or to the movies. The verb has other, figurative uses too.

examples.translation: I'm going to the store.

examples.text: Куда́ вы идёте? — Мы идём домо́й.
examples.translation: Where are you going? — We're going home.
They're going to a concert.
Come here!
A new film is on at the cinema.
It's snowing.

exercises.promptTranslation: I'm going to the store.
Where are you going?

exercises.explanation: Она́ and a singular noun take идёт.
exercises.promptTranslation: Mom is going to the post office.
We're going home.
They're going to a concert.
Yesterday she went home.

exercises.explanation: The command to a friend is иди́.
exercises.promptTranslation: Come here, please!

exercises.prompt: Which preposition and case answer Куда́ ты идёшь? — … магази́н?
What does идёт mean in В кино́ идёт фильм?
exercises.explanation: Идти́ also means “to be on”, for films, lessons and snow.

lessons.title: 38. How you do it: adverbs in -о
lessons.subtitle: Хорошо́, пло́хо, бы́стро, по-ру́сски

explanations.title: From adjective to adverb
explanations.body: An adverb says how, where or when something is done. Many adverbs are made from an adjective by swapping its ending for -о. An adverb never changes. Compare Он хоро́ший студе́нт (adjective, agrees with студе́нт) with Он хорошо́ говори́т (adverb, describes говори́т). A few change a little on the way: плохо́й → пло́хо, лёгкий → легко́.

examples.translation: He speaks Russian well.
She reads quickly.
I write English badly.

explanations.title: In Russian, and how much
explanations.body: To say that you do something in a language, use по- plus the adverb: по-ру́сски, по-англи́йски. Four little words tell how much or how often you do an action: мно́го (a lot), немно́го (a little), ма́ло (little, not enough) and то́лько (only). For now, use them with verbs.

examples.translation: Do you speak Russian?
Yes, a little.
He works a lot.
She doesn't talk much.
We only read.

exercises.explanation: An adverb describes the verb, and never changes.
exercises.promptTranslation: He speaks Russian well.

exercises.explanation: A noun needs an adjective that agrees with it.
exercises.promptTranslation: This is a good student.
She reads quickly.
We speak Russian.

exercises.prompt: Она́ ___ рабо́тает: весь день и весь ве́чер.
exercises.explanation: All day and all evening is a lot.
exercises.promptTranslation: She works a lot: all day and all evening.

exercises.prompt: Я ___ понима́ю по-испа́нски: я зна́ю то́лько «приве́т».
exercises.explanation: Knowing a single word is not enough.
exercises.promptTranslation: I understand little Spanish: I only know “hi”.

exercises.prompt: What is the adverb from плохо́й?
exercises.explanation: Note the stress: it moves to the first syllable.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “I speak English a little”?
exercises.explanation: Use по-…-ски for the language, and немно́го for “a little”.

lessons.title: 39. Sentences with no subject: мо́жно, нельзя́
lessons.subtitle: Здесь мо́жно чита́ть. Здесь краси́во.

explanations.title: Allowed and not allowed
explanations.body: Мо́жно means “it is allowed, one may” and нельзя́ means “it is not allowed, one may not”. Neither has a subject, and the verb that follows is an infinitive. Such sentences are called impersonal. On their own they make a short answer: Мо́жно? — Нельзя́!

examples.translation: May I ask a question?
— May one smoke here? — No, one may not.

explanations.title: It is easy, it was hard
explanations.body: The same idea works with the adverbs you just learned. Russian says Чита́ть легко́ (literally “to read easy”) where English says “It is easy to read”. There is no it and no verb. In the past you add бы́ло, the neuter form of быть, which is why it stays the same whatever the infinitive is.

exercises.explanation: In a library you shouldn't talk loudly.
exercises.promptTranslation: In the library one may not talk loudly.

exercises.explanation: That's the polite way to ask for permission.
exercises.promptTranslation: May I ask a question?

exercises.explanation: It's not allowed at a school.
exercises.promptTranslation: You can't smoke here: this is a school.

exercises.explanation: An impersonal sentence uses the adverb.
exercises.promptTranslation: Reading in Russian is interesting.

exercises.explanation: Impersonal sentences use the neuter бы́ло.
exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday it was interesting.

exercises.explanation: The adverb, with no noun to agree with.
exercises.promptTranslation: It's beautiful here.

exercises.explanation: The past of an impersonal sentence is always бы́ло.
exercises.promptTranslation: It was hard to learn words.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “Smoking is not allowed here”?
exercises.explanation: Нельзя́ is the word for “not allowed”.

lessons.title: 40. Nationalities
lessons.subtitle: Америка́нец, америка́нка, америка́нцы

explanations.title: A noun for a man, one for a woman
explanations.body: Nationalities are nouns, and there is one form for a man, one for a woman, and a plural. They are written with a small letter. The masculine plural is used for a group of men or a mixed group. Watch the spelling: -ец loses its -е- in the plural (не́мец → не́мцы), and -ин drops in англича́не. The exception is ру́сский, which is an adjective used as a noun and agrees like one.

examples.translation: He is American and she is English.
My colleagues are German.
I know an American and a French woman.
All Russians know this song.

exercises.promptTranslation: He is American.
She is German.
They are French.
My mom is French.
We know an American man and an American woman.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “She is German”?

exercises.explanation: Unlike English, Russian writes them with a small letter.

exercises.prompt: Which word is an adjective in form?
exercises.explanation: It agrees with the noun it replaces: ру́сская, ру́сские.

exercises.prompt: A mixed group of men and women: which plural?
exercises.explanation: The masculine plural also covers mixed groups.

lessons.title: 41. Review: verbs, cases and sentences
lessons.subtitle: Putting lessons 21 to 40 together

explanations.title: What do I need?
explanations.body: When you build a sentence, ask yourself a few questions and let the answers choose the form. This is a map of what you have learned since lesson 21.

exercises.promptTranslation: Yesterday she wrote a letter.

exercises.prompt: Ты ви́дишь Анну? — Да, я ви́жу ___.
exercises.explanation: Direct object: accusative, with no preposition so no н.
exercises.promptTranslation: Do you see Anna? — Yes, I see her.
I know the new student.
We're going to the post office.

exercises.explanation: Days take в plus the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: On Friday I'm at home.
Do you speak Russian?

exercises.explanation: A command to ты from the consonant stem пиш-.
exercises.promptTranslation: Write to me!
You can't smoke here: this is a library.

exercises.explanation: Наконе́ц points to a finished result: perfective.
exercises.promptTranslation: I've finally read this book!

exercises.explanation: After a preposition, её becomes неё.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “She is American”?
Which question asks for the destination?

units.title: Unit 7: Habits, walking, having and liking

lessons.title: 42. How often? Always, sometimes, every day
lessons.subtitle: Всегда́, иногда́, ка́ждый день

explanations.title: Words for how often
explanations.body: Russian puts these small adverbs right before the verb, and they never change. Remember that никогда́ (never) needs не before the verb as well: Я никогда́ не рабо́таю там.

explanations.title: Every day, every Saturday
explanations.body: To say “every” plus a time word, use ка́ждый, which agrees with the time word, and put both in the accusative. Masculine and neuter time words do not change; feminine ones end in -ую and -у or -ю. You already know the accusative, so there is nothing new to learn.

examples.translation: Every Saturday I write a letter.
Every day he reads the newspaper.

examples.text: Ка́ждое у́тро мы гуля́ем в па́рке.
examples.translation: Every morning we walk in the park.

exercises.prompt: Она́ ___ чита́ет: ка́ждый день и ка́ждый ве́чер.
exercises.explanation: Every day and every evening means always.
exercises.promptTranslation: She always reads: every day and every evening.

exercises.explanation: A feminine time word after ка́ждую is accusative: -а becomes -у.
exercises.promptTranslation: Every Saturday I'm at home.

exercises.explanation: A masculine time word does not change in the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: Every day we read.

exercises.explanation: A neuter word does not change in the accusative.
exercises.promptTranslation: Every morning he walks in the park.
Every week we write a letter.

exercises.explanation: Никогда́ always comes with не before the verb.
exercises.promptTranslation: I never smoke.

exercises.prompt: Which adverb is the most frequent?

exercises.explanation: Воскресе́нье is neuter, so ка́ждое, and neuter nouns don't change in the accusative.

lessons.title: 43. Two verbs for walking: идти́ and ходи́ть
lessons.subtitle: Иду́ сейча́с, хожу́ ка́ждый день

explanations.title: One way now, or back and forth
explanations.body: Russian has two verbs for going on foot. Идти́ is for one trip in one direction: you are on your way somewhere right now, or you have a destination in mind. Ходи́ть is for everything else: habits and repeated trips, going and coming back, general ability, and walking around with no particular direction. Words like ка́ждый день, обы́чно and ча́сто point to ходи́ть. Words like сейча́с and the question Куда́? point to идти́.

rows: back and forth, or in general
Я хожу́ в магази́н ка́ждый день.

explanations.title: Ходи́ть: forms and the past
explanations.body: Ходи́ть is a second-family verb with the я-form change you met in lesson 24 (д becomes ж). In the past, ходи́л в парк means “went to the park (and came back)”, so it can replace был: Вчера́ я ходи́л в парк = Вчера́ я был в па́рке. For commands, ходи́ть is the usual verb for a negative command (Не ходи́!), and идти́ for a positive one (Иди́!).

examples.text: Ка́ждый день мы хо́дим в парк.
examples.translation: Every day we go to the park.
Where are you going (now)?
Don't go to the store today.
Go home!
It's raining. (always идти́)

exercises.explanation: Every day = a habit, so ходи́ть.
exercises.promptTranslation: Every day I go to the park.

exercises.explanation: Сейча́с = right now, one direction: идти́.
exercises.promptTranslation: Right now I'm going to the store.
We often go to the movies.

exercises.explanation: Right now, to a destination: идти́.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where are you going right now?

exercises.explanation: A general activity (no particular trip): ходи́ть. After люблю́ use the infinitive.
exercises.promptTranslation: I like to walk fast.

exercises.explanation: A negative command normally uses ходи́ть.
exercises.promptTranslation: Don't go to the store today!

exercises.explanation: A positive command normally uses идти́.
exercises.promptTranslation: Go home!

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “Yesterday I went to the institute (and came back)”?
exercises.explanation: Past ходи́л = a completed round trip, like был.

exercises.prompt: Which verb is always used for “It's raining”?
exercises.explanation: Идёт дождь, идёт снег, идёт уро́к: always идти́.

lessons.title: 44. Talking about: о and об
lessons.subtitle: Я ду́маю о рабо́те, Мы говори́м об учи́теле

explanations.title: О + the prepositional case
explanations.body: The preposition о (about, of) always takes the prepositional case. It comes after verbs of thinking and talking: ду́мать, говори́ть, расска́зывать (to tell), разгова́ривать (to chat), чита́ть (to read about). The questions are О чём? (about what?) and О ком? (about whom?). Remember that the prepositional ends in -е for most nouns.

examples.text: О чём вы ду́маете? — Я ду́маю о рабо́те.
examples.translation: What are you thinking about? — I'm thinking about work.
He tells about his family.

explanations.title: Before a vowel, об
explanations.body: When the next word starts with а, и, о, у or э, о becomes об, to keep the vowels apart. You say об учи́теле, об отце́, об э́той кни́ге, об а́вгусте. Before consonants it stays о: о ком, о бра́те. Never use об before a consonant.

examples.text: О ком вы говори́те? — Мы говори́м об учи́теле.
examples.translation: Whom are you talking about? — We're talking about the teacher.
I'm reading about this book.
They're chatting about [their] father.

exercises.explanation: After о the noun is prepositional: -а becomes -е.
exercises.promptTranslation: I'm thinking about work.
We're talking about [my] brother.
She tells about her family.

exercises.explanation: Учи́теле starts with у, so о becomes об.
exercises.promptTranslation: He's talking about the teacher.

exercises.explanation: Отце́ starts with о, so об.
exercises.promptTranslation: They're talking about [their] father.

exercises.explanation: Э́той starts with э, so об.
exercises.promptTranslation: We're reading about this book.
What are you thinking about?

exercises.explanation: Ком starts with к, a consonant: о.
exercises.promptTranslation: Whom are you talking about?

exercises.prompt: Which case follows о in the meaning “about”?

options: Before а, и, о, у, э
exercises.explanation: To avoid two vowels in a row.

lessons.title: 45. There is, there are: е́сть
lessons.subtitle: В го́роде есть река́

explanations.title: Saying something exists
explanations.body: To say that something exists or is available somewhere, put the place first, then есть, then the thing. Есть never changes (it stands for both is and are), and the thing that follows is in the nominative, singular or plural. The sentence works like a map: place, then what is in it.

examples.translation: Is there a telephone here?
Yes, there is.
There are big stores on the street.

explanations.title: Есть or где?
explanations.body: Use есть to introduce something that may or may not be there: В го́роде есть мост. Use Где? and вот when you already know the thing and are asking about its location: Где мой телефо́н? — Вот он. For the past tense you use был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли instead of есть, as in lesson 19.

examples.translation: Where is my phone? — Here it is.
There was a bridge in the city.

exercises.promptTranslation: There is a market in the city.
There's a hotel on the street.

exercises.explanation: The thing after есть is nominative.
exercises.promptTranslation: There's a table and a chair in the room.
There are big stores on the street.

exercises.explanation: To point at something you already know about, use вот.
exercises.promptTranslation: Where's my phone? — Here it is!

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means “There is a bridge in our city”?
exercises.explanation: Place first, then есть, then the thing.

exercises.prompt: How do you answer “Is there a hotel here?” briefly and positively?
In what case is the noun after есть?
exercises.explanation: В ко́мнате есть стол: стол is nominative.

exercises.prompt: How do you say “There was a bridge in the city”?
exercises.explanation: In the past, быть agrees with the thing: мост is masculine.

lessons.title: 46. I have: у меня́ есть
lessons.subtitle: У меня́ есть брат, у неё есть маши́на

explanations.title: “At me there is”
explanations.body: Russian has no verb “to have” for owning things. It says “at me there is”: у меня́ есть. The person goes after у in a special form, and the thing you have is in the nominative. These forms look like the accusative pronouns you know, and the same rule adds a н when a preposition comes before его́, её or их.

explanations.title: When есть is left out
explanations.body: Use есть when the point is that you have something at all. If the sentence mostly describes the thing (a new car, a big family), есть is dropped and the description comes first: У него́ но́вая маши́на. У нас больша́я семья́. In the past, use был, была́, бы́ло, бы́ли, which agree with the thing you had.

examples.translation: I have a car. (the fact of having one)
I have a new car. (describing it)
She has a big family.
We had a car.

exercises.promptTranslation: I have a brother.
Do you have a car?
